Every release has two steps: upload the new assets under versioned names, then switch the manifest to point at those names. The manifest tells browsers which assets to load.

**Why the upload comes first:** The moment the manifest switches, browsers start requesting the names it lists. If those files were not already uploaded, those requests would fail and users would get a broken page. Uploading first means every name the new manifest points to already exists when the switch happens.

**Why we keep the old assets:** Some browsers loaded the previous manifest before the switch and will keep requesting the old names it lists. If we deleted those files, those users would get missing scripts or styles partway through their session. Keeping the old assets lets those sessions finish on the version they started with.

Versioned names are what make both steps safe. Because new files never overwrite old ones, the two versions can sit side by side, and the manifest switch is the single point where traffic moves from one to the other.

A release happens in two steps: first we upload every new asset under a versioned name, then we switch the manifest to point at those names.

The upload comes first so the manifest never references a file that isn't there yet. As soon as the manifest switches, browsers start requesting whatever it names. If we switched first, some browsers would request new asset names before those files existed and get broken pages. Uploading first means every name in the new manifest already resolves when the switch happens.

We keep the old assets because switching the manifest doesn't update browsers that already loaded the previous one. Those browsers keep requesting the old versioned names, for example when they lazy-load a script or fetch an image later in the session. If we deleted the old files, those requests would fail mid-session. Keeping them lets those browsers finish with a consistent old set, while new page loads get the new set.

Versioned names make both of these possible. Old and new files never overwrite each other, so both sets can be live at the same time, and the manifest switch is the single moment the release takes effect.

A release has two steps: upload every new asset under a versioned name, then switch the manifest to point at those names.

The upload comes first because the manifest switch is what makes a release live. Once a browser fetches the new manifest, it immediately requests whatever names it lists. If those files were still uploading, the browser would get 404s or a half-loaded page. Uploading everything first means every name in the new manifest already resolves when the switch happens. The switch itself becomes a single step that turns the release on.

We keep the old assets because browsers don't all move to the new manifest at once. A page that loaded before the switch still holds the previous manifest and will keep requesting the old names, for example when it lazy-loads a script or image later. If those files were deleted, those users would hit broken requests mid-session. Leaving the old versions in place lets every browser finish with a consistent set of files, whichever manifest it fetched.

Versioned names make both of these safe. New files never overwrite old ones, so both releases can sit side by side.

Each release happens in two steps: first we upload every new asset under a versioned name (for example `app.3f9c2a.js`), then we switch the manifest to point at those new names.

The upload comes first so that the manifest never references anything missing. Once the manifest switches, browsers immediately start requesting the files it names. If any of those files weren't uploaded yet, those requests would fail and users would see broken pages. Because new assets use new names, uploading them early is safe: nothing references them until the switch, so the live site is unaffected.

We keep the old assets because some browsers already loaded the previous manifest and will keep requesting the files it names, such as a tab opened before the release that later lazy-loads a script. If we deleted the old files at switch time, those requests would fail mid-session. Since each version has its own names, old and new files can coexist, and both groups of users get a consistent set of files.
